subject: Business
title: When to Pivot vs. Persist
description: A quick win: understand When to Pivot vs. Persist.

hook.text: Slack started as a video game company. The game failed, but the internal chat tool took off.

buildup.text: A pivot means changing strategy while keeping one foot planted in what you've already learned.

discovery.text: Instagram pivoted from a check-in app called Burbn. They kept the photo feature nobody expected.

twist.text: Not every struggle means pivot. Sometimes you're one iteration away from a breakthrough.

climax.text: The test: are you getting closer to product-market fit each cycle, or just running in circles?

punchline.text: A pivot isn't giving up. It's choosing which door to open.

quiz.question: What signal suggests it's time to pivot?
options: Repeated cycles show no progress toward product-market fit

details.summary: The decision to pivot versus persist is the hardest judgment call in entrepreneurship. Pivoting changes strategy while preserving learning, but pivoting too early abandons promising directions while persisting too long wastes resources on dead ends. Data, not hope, should drive the decision.
details.whyItMatters: Most successful companies pivoted at least once. But premature pivoting means never giving an idea enough time to work, while stubborn persistence burns capital on lost causes.
takeaways: Pivot when data shows fundamental assumptions are wrong, not just because growth is slow
Persist when core metrics are improving even if the pace feels frustratingly slow
Most successful startups pivoted at least once before finding product-market fit

faq.question: What signals indicate it is time to pivot?
faq.answer: Engagement metrics are flat or declining despite significant product iterations. Customer interviews consistently reveal a different problem than the one you are solving. A side feature generates more excitement than the core product.

faq.question: What signals indicate you should persist despite slow progress?
faq.answer: Retention is improving even if acquisition is slow. Users who discover the product love it. The market is growing in your direction. You have identified specific friction points that, if fixed, would unlock growth. Core engagement metrics trend positively even if absolute numbers are small.
